The method an AI uses to solve a problem is what really matters.​
Is it simply brute-forcing known patterns to arrive at a solution, or does it actually understand what it’s doing: creating new patterns and generating novel solutions that can be applied elsewhere?​
The former is more like an advanced calculator; the latter is closer to true intelligence.​
Both approaches can produce correct answers and valid proofs, but when it comes to evaluating AGI, the proof itself isn’t the meaningful part, but rather the reasoning path is​

comments.text: Short clear wording is good. Short wording that can easily be misunderstood is bad. Words have two functions, they are both the carrier and the cargo. It is important to carry spoken language through noise and mis-hearings and to carry written language through transcription errors and mis-readings. The cargo is the meaning of the words. The type of speech used by the model discussed here is a weak carrier, but the cargo is good.

comments.author: @katsup_07
comments.text:
Do the reasoning models actually reason or are they brute force computing more?
Here is an analogy below about intelligence vs brute force to help understand the difference.

The Lock Picker vs. The Locksmith
Imagine two people trying to open a locked safe:

The Locksmith
- Understands how locks work.
- Analyzes the type of lock and its mechanism.
- Applies principles of engineering and logic.
- Opens the lock with a custom-made method.

-> This is true reasoning: based on understanding, abstraction, and generalization.

The Lock Picker
- Doesn’t understand how locks work.
- Just tries millions of combinations, extremely fast.
- Eventually stumbles on one that opens the safe.

-> This is brute-force pattern matching, effective, but not intelligent.

Both succeed, but only one understands. The brute-force solution looks smart from the outside, but lacks internal understanding or transferability. 

Is an LLM more like a locksmith or a lock picker? That is what I am wondering about.

" ... project that forward ...*

Indeed. I run into people all the time who are certain that these models absolutely can not do a bunch of things that they've been able to do for at least a year now. 

But project forward these models' current ability to learn from interactions with the world (including humans), commit that info to persistent memory, and then send that info upstream, to update the underlying models' weights -- and you get ... NOTHING. The models are still static. Frozen. Big context windows are cool, but that only practically scales so far. We don't have a situation analogous to meat brain plasticity. 

We have seen ZERO developments in continuous learning -- or at least zero that have shown up in available products.
